subtype: Wide eyes in wonder and fear [Expressing]
passage: Park note, Monday. Mehak, nearly two, was sitting in the sandpit when a large brown dog trotted by on a lead. Her eyes went wide and she went still. Then she turned and looked straight at my face. I kept my voice calm, smiled and said, “That's a dog, and his owner is holding him.” Her shoulders dropped, and she pointed. I stayed beside her while she watched him leave. Next time we will watch from further away first and see how she feels. 🙂

qa.q: Where was Mehak when the dog passed?
qa.a: In the sandpit at the park.

qa.q: Why did Mehak look at the narrator's face after seeing the dog?
qa.a: She was probably checking whether the dog was safe, and her wide eyes could show fascination or alarm. Her dropped shoulders after the narrator's calm words suggest she felt reassured.

qa.q: What is the narrator's plan for next time and why is it sensible?
qa.a: They will start further from the dog and see how Mehak reacts. That lets Mehak approach the new sight at her own pace.

qa.q: How might the dog owner's calm hold on the lead matter to Mehak?
qa.a: Seeing the lead may help Mehak feel the dog is under control, and the owner's relaxed manner adds to the narrator's calm message.

grounding: A toddler widens her eyes at something new and checks the caregiver's face to decide between wonder and alarm.

subtype: Wide eyes in wonder and fear [Expressing]
passage: A peacock stepped onto the mud path in front of the house, fanning half its tail. Charu, two, stopped with her eyes stretched wide. She held her breath and looked at the huge bird, then swung round to see her aunt Lavanya's face. Lavanya was smiling at the peacock. “Mor,” she said softly. Charu's shoulders dropped, and she took one careful step towards it, then another, eyes still wide, one hand reaching behind her for the edge of Lavanya's saree.

qa.q: What did Charu see on the mud path?
qa.a: A peacock with its tail half fanned.

qa.q: What might Charu have felt when she looked back at Lavanya, and what could it mean otherwise?
qa.a: She was probably checking whether the peacock was safe. Her wide eyes could mean fascination or a little alarm, and her stepping forward while holding the saree suggests both.

qa.q: What could Lavanya do to help Charu enjoy the moment?
qa.a: She could stay close, keep her calm smile, and let Charu decide how near to go.

qa.q: What might have happened if Lavanya had looked frightened?
qa.a: Charu might have taken it as a sign the bird was dangerous and backed away, so the wonder could have turned into fear.

grounding: A toddler widens her eyes at something new and looks to the caregiver for a reaction to decide between wonder and fear.
